## Problem E8: Adiabatic Water Gas Shift Reactor {.unnumbered}

The water gas shift reaction is used in hydrogen and ammonia plants to convert carbon monoxide in synthesis gas into additional hydrogen:

$$\mathrm{CO(g)} + \mathrm{H_2O(g)} \rightleftharpoons \mathrm{CO_2(g)} + \mathrm{H_2(g)}$$

A high-temperature shift converter is a packed bed of iron-chromium catalyst. It is heavily lagged and operates adiabatically — there is no cooling inside the bed, so all the energy released by the reaction appears as a temperature rise across the reactor.

Synthesis gas enters the reactor at 350 °C at the following rates:

| Species | Feed rate / mol s$\hb{^{-1}}$ |
|---|---|
| $\mathrm{CO}$ | 20 |
| $\mathrm{H_2O}$ (g) | 60 |
| $\mathrm{N_2}$ (inert) | 20 |

80% of the carbon monoxide fed is converted. The following data are provided:

| Species | Enthalpy of formation / kJ mol$\hb{^{-1}}$ | Heat capacity / J mol$\hb{^{-1}}$ K$\hb{^{-1}}$ |
|---|---|---|
| $\mathrm{CO}$ (g) | −110.5 | 29.1 |
| $\mathrm{H_2O}$ (g) | −241.8 | 34.0 |
| $\mathrm{CO_2}$ (g) | −393.5 | 41.3 |
| $\mathrm{H_2}$ (g) | 0 | 29.0 |
| $\mathrm{N_2}$ (g) | 0 | 29.1 |

**(a)** Calculate the enthalpy of reaction ($\Delta H^\circ_{rxn}$) at 298.15 K and state whether the reaction is exothermic or endothermic.

**(b)** Calculate the extent of reaction and the molar flow rate of every species leaving the reactor.

**(c)** Starting from the general energy balance, write down and simplify the steady-state energy balance for the reactor. Show that it reduces to a sum of $\Delta H$ terms equal to zero, and state the path you will use to evaluate them. Note that the feed does **not** enter at 298.15 K.

**(d)** Calculate the reactor outlet temperature.

**(e)** The steam-to-CO ratio in the feed is 3:1, well above the 1:1 required by stoichiometry. Recalculate the outlet temperature for a 1:1 feed (20 mol s$^{-1}$ of steam) at the same 80% conversion, and explain the role the excess steam is playing.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}

::: {.callout-note icon=false collapse="true" title="Solution"}

**(a) Enthalpy of reaction**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Delta H^\circ_{rxn} & = \sum \nu_j\,\Delta H^\circ_{f,j} \\
                     & = \left[(-393.5) + 0\right] - \left[(-110.5) + (-241.8)\right] \\
                     & = -393.5 + 352.3 \\
                     & = -41.2\ \text{kJ/mol}
\end{aligned}
$$

The reaction is **exothermic**, though only mildly so — about 5% of the energy released by burning the same amount of carbon monoxide completely.

**(b) Extent of reaction and outlet flows**

$$\dot{\xi} = 0.80 \times 20 = 16\ \text{mol/s}$$

The stoichiometric coefficients are all $\pm 1$, so each species changes by $\dot{\xi}$:

| Species | In / mol s$\hb{^{-1}}$ | Change | Out / mol s$\hb{^{-1}}$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\mathrm{CO}$ | 20 | $-\dot{\xi}$ | 4 |
| $\mathrm{H_2O}$ (g) | 60 | $-\dot{\xi}$ | 44 |
| $\mathrm{CO_2}$ (g) | 0 | $+\dot{\xi}$ | 16 |
| $\mathrm{H_2}$ (g) | 0 | $+\dot{\xi}$ | 16 |
| $\mathrm{N_2}$ | 20 | 0 | 20 |
| **Total** | **100** | | **100** |

The total molar flow is unchanged, since the reaction converts two moles into two moles.

**(c) Energy balance**

Assumptions:

- Steady state $\Rightarrow \dfrac{d(m_{sys}H_{sys})}{dt} = 0$.
- Adiabatic (heavily lagged) $\Rightarrow \dot{Q} = 0$.
- No shaft work $\Rightarrow \dot{W} = 0$.
- Heat capacities constant over the temperature range; pressure effects on enthalpy neglected.

Starting from the general energy balance:

$$\frac{d(m_{sys}H_{sys})}{dt} = \sum \dot{n}_{in}H_{in} - \sum \dot{n}_{out}H_{out} + \dot{Q} + \dot{W}$$

$$0 = \sum \dot{n}_{in}H_{in} - \sum \dot{n}_{out}H_{out}$$

$$\Delta \dot{H} = \sum \dot{n}_{out}H_{out} - \sum \dot{n}_{in}H_{in} = 0$$

So the total enthalpy change from inlet state to outlet state is zero. Enthalpy is a state function, so any path between those two states gives the same answer. The only temperature at which the reaction enthalpy is known is 298.15 K, so the convenient path is:

1. **Cool the feed** from 623.15 K to 298.15 K.
2. **React** at 298.15 K, to an extent $\dot{\xi}$.
3. **Heat the products** from 298.15 K to the unknown outlet temperature $T_{out}$.

$$\Delta \dot{H} = \underbrace{\sum_i \dot{n}_{in,i}C_{P,i}(298.15 - T_{in})}_{\Delta \dot{H}_1} + \underbrace{\dot{\xi}\,\Delta H^\circ_{rxn}}_{\Delta \dot{H}_2} + \underbrace{\sum_j \dot{n}_{out,j}C_{P,j}(T_{out} - 298.15)}_{\Delta \dot{H}_3} = 0$$

Every term is an enthalpy *difference*, so no reference state is needed.

**(d) Outlet temperature**

*Step 1 — cool the feed to 298.15 K:*

| Species | $\hb{\dot{n}_{in}}$ / mol s$\hb{^{-1}}$ | $\hb{C_P}$ / J mol$\hb{^{-1}}$ K$\hb{^{-1}}$ | $\hb{\dot{n}C_P}$ / kW K$\hb{^{-1}}$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\mathrm{CO}$ | 20 | 29.1 | 0.582 |
| $\mathrm{H_2O}$ (g) | 60 | 34.0 | 2.040 |
| $\mathrm{N_2}$ | 20 | 29.1 | 0.582 |
| **Total** | | | **3.204** |

$$\Delta \dot{H}_1 = 3.204 \times (298.15 - 623.15) = 3.204 \times (-325) = -1041.3\ \text{kJ/s}$$

*Step 2 — react at 298.15 K:*

$$\Delta \dot{H}_2 = \dot{\xi}\,\Delta H^\circ_{rxn} = 16 \times (-41.2) = -659.2\ \text{kJ/s}$$

*Step 3 — heat the products:*

| Species | $\hb{\dot{n}_{out}}$ / mol s$\hb{^{-1}}$ | $\hb{C_P}$ / J mol$\hb{^{-1}}$ K$\hb{^{-1}}$ | $\hb{\dot{n}C_P}$ / kW K$\hb{^{-1}}$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\mathrm{CO}$ | 4 | 29.1 | 0.116 |
| $\mathrm{H_2O}$ (g) | 44 | 34.0 | 1.496 |
| $\mathrm{CO_2}$ | 16 | 41.3 | 0.661 |
| $\mathrm{H_2}$ | 16 | 29.0 | 0.464 |
| $\mathrm{N_2}$ | 20 | 29.1 | 0.582 |
| **Total** | | | **3.319** |

Setting the sum to zero and rearranging symbolically:

$$T_{out} = 298.15 + \frac{-\left(\Delta \dot{H}_1 + \Delta \dot{H}_2\right)}{\sum_j \dot{n}_{out,j}C_{P,j}}$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
T_{out} & = 298.15 + \frac{1041.3 + 659.2}{3.319} \\
        & = 298.15 + \frac{1700.5}{3.319} \\
        & = 298.15 + 512.3 \\
        & = 810.5\ \text{K}\ (537.3\ ^\circ\text{C})
\end{aligned}
$$

The adiabatic temperature rise across the bed is therefore $537.3 - 350 = 187\ ^\circ\text{C}$.

**Sanity check:** the reaction is exothermic and the reactor is adiabatic, so the outlet must be hotter than the inlet.

**(e) The effect of the steam-to-CO ratio**

With 20 mol/s of steam instead of 60, and the same $\dot{\xi} = 16$ mol/s:

Feed: $\mathrm{CO}$ 20, $\mathrm{H_2O}$ 20, $\mathrm{N_2}$ 20 mol/s.
$$\sum \dot{n}_{in}C_{P,i} = 0.582 + 0.680 + 0.582 = 1.844\ \text{kW/K}$$
$$\Delta \dot{H}_1 = 1.844 \times (-325) = -599.3\ \text{kJ/s}$$

Outlet: $\mathrm{CO}$ 4, $\mathrm{H_2O}$ 4, $\mathrm{CO_2}$ 16, $\mathrm{H_2}$ 16, $\mathrm{N_2}$ 20 mol/s.
$$\sum \dot{n}_{out}C_{P,j} = 0.116 + 0.136 + 0.661 + 0.464 + 0.582 = 1.959\ \text{kW/K}$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
T_{out} & = 298.15 + \frac{599.3 + 659.2}{1.959} \\
        & = 298.15 + 642.4 \\
        & = 940.6\ \text{K}\ (667.4\ ^\circ\text{C})
\end{aligned}
$$

The adiabatic rise jumps from 187 $^\circ$C to 317 $^\circ$C.

The excess steam is acting as **thermal resistance**. It takes no part in the energy release (the same 659 kJ/s is liberated in both cases) but it nearly doubles the heat capacity of the gas that this energy must heat, so the same enthalpy release produces a much smaller temperature rise.
